Waiver Request – 611 Holdings II Storage Yard Mr. Bruce Howe of Vista Design and Mr. Mark Spencer Cropper, the applicant’s attorney, approached the table. Mr. Howe provided a brief overview of the project and summarized the requests being made. Two waivers were requested: one from the paving requirements to allow gravel within the storage yard, and another from the screening requirements to allow a chainlink fence with privacy slats to be used in lieu of landscaping. Mr. Cropper gave a brief history of the project’s proceedings with the Board of Appeals, noting that multiple variances and special exceptions were previously granted for the use of the property as a storage yard, the installation of a privacy fence, and relief from the front-yard setback requirements. Following a brief discussion, Mr. French noted that he believes a fence with privacy slats by itself does not fit the neighborhood and believes the applicant should move forward with landscaped screening or possibly a more aesthetically pleasing fence material. Other members of the commission concurred. Steve Engel from Vista Design approached the table. He mentioned concerns about the landscaping being destroyed when SHA does maintenance and mows the lawns along the highways. Mr. Barbierri found it necessary to move forward with the gravel waiver request before continuing the discussion about the landscaping waiver. The Commission moved to grant the waiver request for the application of gravel on the lot motioned by Mrs. Ott and seconded by Mr. French, and the motion was approved unanimously. Further discussion regarding the landscaped screening waiver continued. Following this, Mr. Cropper decided to withdraw the waiver from the landscaping, and discuss steps to move forward with the applicant with plans to return at a later date. IV. Waiver Request –10529 Flower St / Build Pines LLC– Contractor Shops Hugh Cropper, attorney for Build Pines LLC, and Ben Sharp, owner of Build Pines LLC, approached the table. Mr. Cropper provided a brief overview of the project and its location. Two waivers were requested: a waiver from the paving requirements to allow gravel in the driving and parking areas, and a waiver from the screening requirements, as the proposed buildings will be screened from view by existing forest After some brief discussion Mr. French motioned to approval the waiver for the landscaping screening requirements, seconded by Mrs. Wimbrow and the motion was approved unanimously. Atlantic Coastal Bays Growth Allocation Request – Salt Life Park (Phase 3) Mr. Hugh Cropper, attorney, Chris McCabe, Coastal Compliance Solutions LLC, Steve Engel, Vista Design Inc., and Mark Odachowski, owner of Salt Life Phase III approached the table. Mr. Cropper gave an overview of the existing Salt Life Community and provided a history of the property for which the growth allocation requested. He then provided background on the Coastal Bays Critical Area program and growth allocation requests in general. Mr. Cropper also explained the standards for growth allocation in the Critical Area law as well as the new standards related to environmental justice and resiliency. Mr. Cropper questioned Mr. Engel to confirm that the growth allocation request meets the standards in the Critical Area law. Mr. Engel confirmed that the request meets or exceeds the standards. Mr. Cropper questioned Mr. Odachowski about the economic benefit that the existing Salt Life Community has had in the area. Mr. Odachowski stated he believes there has been a positive economic impact. Mr. Cropper questioned Mr. McCabe on the environmental impacts associated with the proposed growth allocation. Mr. McCabe confirmed that the environmental impacts were minimal and all required mitigation and stormwater requirements would be met. Mr. Cropper finished his presentation by stating the growth allocation request and proposed development are good examples of infill development and an appropriate use of the County’s allotted growth allocation acreage. Mr. Barbierri asked Mr. McCabe to explain the new standards of environmental justice and resilience. Mr. McCabe stated that the only metric that exceeded the threshold for environmental justice was low birth rate. He explained how the developer worked with Worcester County Parks and Recreation to perform the mitigation at Homer Gudelsky Park and the Herring Creek Nature Park benefiting residents. Mrs. Phyllis Wimbrow asked if the owner was aware growth allocation would be needed when the zoning map amendment was approved in 2025. Mr. Cropper replied that the Critical Area designation was discussed by the Planning Commission and County Commissioners at their respective meetings. Mr. Alec French asked if the owner was aware of the Critical Area and zoning regulations, specifically the density, when he purchased the property. Mr. Odachowski and Mr. Cropper stated the property was purchased in 1999 prior to the existence of the Atlantic Coastal Bays Critical Area. Page 3 of 5 WORCESTER COUNTY PLANNING COMMISSION MEETING MINUTES – October 1, 2026 Mr. Cropper explained how growth allocation is calculated and how the allocation is awarded. Mr. Brian Soper stated there will be 360 acres of growth allocation for the coastal bays remaining if this request is approved. Mr. French voiced his concerns about the environmental impacts of the growth allocation and the development associated with it. Mr. Cropper explained how the proposed development meets all the standards of growth allocation and the intent of the comprehensive plan. Mrs. Wimbrow stated she shared the concerns of Mr. French however she explained how the proposed development is consistent with the comprehensive plan and zoning in addition to bringing affordable housing to the area. A motion was made by Mrs. Marlene Ott to forward a favorable recommendation. The motion was seconded by Mrs. Wimbrow, and the motion was approved 5-1 with Mr. French opposing. VI. Text Amendment - §Z 1-303 CA Commercial Airport District Zachary Williams, Venable, attorney for the applicants; Rob Corradi and Ellis Harkins, Amazon, applicants; Jeremey Sweeny, applicant, Maryland Broadband Cooperative (MdBC) board member; and Drew Van Dopp, CEO MdBC, were present for the review. Mr. Corradi explained that the text amendment concerns a power feed equipment (PFE) building, not a cable landing station (CLS) or data center, which are subject to the moratorium. The proposal is for one 1,200-square-foot building on a 3,500-square-foot site at the airport. The building would not connect to public water or sewer and is being developed with the Maryland Broadband Cooperative (MdBC). Mr. Williams said the applicants had provided an additional letter addressing public comments and expected to answer questions about the project. The Planning Commission asked about Globalinx’s involvement, lease agreements between Amazon and Ocean City, and contracts between Amazon and MdBC. The applicants clarified that the building’s size and power limits would allow it to serve only one subsea cable. It would boost fiber-optic signals between the subsea cable, overseas connections, and fiber lines to the Washington area. They stated that no CLS or data center is planned for Worcester County. Cable manufacturing is beginning, with installation anticipated in late 2027, pending required permits and approvals. Commission members asked about the cable’s right-of-way, potential conflicts with other utilities, and local benefits. The applicants said they are working with MdBC to connect the cable to Washington and that it would expand broadband capacity without requiring local funding. Mr. Van Dopp explained that the project could create more reliable fiber pathways, Page 4 of 5 WORCESTER COUNTY PLANNING COMMISSION MEETING MINUTES – October 1, 2026 reduce service bottlenecks on the Eastern Shore, and benefit highways, schools, health care providers, and local businesses. Further discussion focused on the project’s technical requirements, community benefits, and costs. Although the proposed building appeared limited in scope, commissioners recognized that the application is very technical and could have significant community impacts. The Planning Commission confirmed that staff could not reject the application. However, because the zoning code requires a recommendation only “within a reasonable time,” it does not establish a specific deadline. Ms. Wimbrow moved to postpone consideration of the text amendment for 60 days to allow additional study. Ms. Drew seconded the motion, which passed unanimously, with Mr. Barbierri, Mr. French, Ms. Purnell-Milbourne, and Ms. Ott voting in favor. Next step: The Planning Commission will revisit the text amendment request at a future meeting, no sooner than December 2026. VII.
